newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Congo's capital stays calm for second morning.
newsitem.headline: Congo's capital stays calm for second morning.

text.p: Congo's capital Brazzaville, devastated by 12 days of faction fighting, enjoyed a second morning of calm on Thursday as a 72-hour ceasefire held firm.
A U.N. envoy who met both warring leaders on Wednesday said they had agreed to extend the truce as long as they could after the original deal expires at midnight Friday.

"The political leaders assured me that they would give instructions to their troops and to their military negotiators to prolong the ceasefire as long as possible," Mohamed Sahnoun said before flying to brief peace mediators in next-door Gabon.
He urged France not to proceed with a planned withdrawal of all its 1,250 troops in the city until a proposed African or international intervention force could replace them.
Residents and Western officials said by telephone that the paralysed city, facing the former Zaire's capital Kinshasa across the giant Congo river, was peaceful early on Thursday.

"There's no shooting, one hears nothing," said one resident near to city centre front lines, where the forces of President Pascal Lissouba and foes backing his once Marxist predecessor, Denis Sassou Nguesso, eye each other nervously.

He said some people who fled to a southern suburb held by city mayor Bernard Kolelas, a third strongman who has kept out of the fighting, had managed to sneak home across the lines to get food from their freezers and salvage other belongings.

If the peace holds, Red Cross volunteers are due to begin on Thursday with the gruesome task of recovering an estimated several hundred bodies that are rotting in the streets where no one has dared go.

The aid workers have been promised a passage through the front line that divides Lissouba's rump government forces with his "Zulu" militia from Sassou Nguesso's "Cobras", who started fighting when Lissouba tried to disarm them on June 5.
Sahnoun said the sight of so many bodies, mainly civilians cut down in the crossfire, had sickened him.

He told reporters as he left the former French colonial capital that an intervention force was a realistic idea but the biggest danger was what would happen if the warring militias were left on their own before it was in place.
"The problem is going to be when the peace force can be deployed. I'm much more afraid of the vacuum that could exist in the short term," said the U.N. envoy for central Africa.

France's Figaro newspaper said the three-day truce had been brokered by Paris' ambassador in Brazzaville and speculated it could be just to ease the pullout of the French troops who evacuated some 5,500 foreigners during the fighting.
French General Rene Landrin said on Wednesday that around half of his men had already left and that the rest would leave as planned by Sunday at the latest.
There was no immediate reaction from Paris to Sahnoun's appeal for them to stay.

Sahnoun said Lissouba, whose election victory in 1992 ended Sassou Nguesso's 13-year rule, was in favour of an African intervention force. His rival had expressed some reservations but said he had no objections in principle.
The two rivals, along with Kolelas, were seen as the frontrunners for fresh presidential elections for the end of July which the fighting has rendered unholdable.
Local radio said three observers from each side would sit in the control tower of the airport, which the French still control, to verify efforts to turn it into a demilitarised zone.
The fighting has spared the rest of the oil-rich country.
